`earliest_start` is this much after `never`, and `latest_end` this much
before `forever`.

Examples:
    ~~~hgl
    assert smallest_step == 1us
    assert earliest_start - never == smallest_step
    ~~~

documentation.text:
The capability a node has by `inject clock`: the times of the run as the node is evaluated.

A clock has properties and no operation. A node uses it in its hooks,
and may give it to a parameter of type `Clock` of a `const fn`; it does
not retain it. Nothing in a program constructs one.

A property is read as an ordinary value and is not assigned.

Examples:
    The clock is given to a `const fn`, which reads the time of each
    input tick. Each column of the trace is one microsecond.

    ~~~hgl
    const fn stamped(clock: Clock, value: i64) -> tuple<datetime, i64> =>
        (clock.evaluation_time, value)

    fn time_of_input(value: i64) -> tuple<datetime, i64> {
        inject clock
        when { return stamped(clock, value) }
    }

    let t = @2026-01-05T09:30:00Z
    assert eval{start: t} time_of_input(value: [10, _, 20]) ==
        [(t, 10), _, (t + 2us, 20)]
    ~~~

Rules:
    CAP-1, CAP-3, CAP-4, CAP-8, CRUN-3, TIME-8
documentation.summary: The capability a node has by `inject clock`: the times of the run as the node is evaluated.

documentation.text:
The logical time shared by every node throughout the current cycle.

In `start` it is the run's start time. In `stop` it retains the last
cycle's time. Each cycle advances by at least `smallest_step`.

Examples:
    In `start` the evaluation time is the run's start time. The node
    keeps it in a `cache` and returns it at the input's first tick.

    ~~~hgl
    fn started_at(value: i64) -> datetime {
        inject clock
        cache first: datetime = never
        start { first = clock.evaluation_time }
        when { return first }
    }

    let t = @2026-01-05T09:30:00Z
    assert eval{start: t} started_at(value: [_, 1]) == [_, t]
    ~~~

Rules:
    CAP-3, CAP-8, CRUN-3, TIME-8
documentation.summary: The logical time shared by every node throughout the current cycle.

documentation.text:
The engine's estimate of wall-clock time at the point of the read.

In real time this is the computer's UTC clock. In simulation it is
`Clock.evaluation_time` plus `Clock.cycle_time`. It may change
between reads. A scheduler wake with `on_wall_clock: true` uses
this clock in real time.

Examples:
    ~~~hgl
    fn at_or_after_cycle(value: i64) -> bool {
        inject clock
        when { return clock.now >= clock.evaluation_time }
    }
    assert eval at_or_after_cycle(value: [1, _, 2]) == [true, _, true]
    ~~~

Rules:
    CAP-3, CAP-4, CAP-8, TIME-8

documentation.text:
The earliest evaluation time the next cycle could have.

It is `Clock.evaluation_time` plus `smallest_step`. Reading it
does not schedule a cycle.

Examples:
    The next cycle could come one smallest step later.

    ~~~hgl
    fn next_step(value: i64) -> bool {
        inject clock
        when {
            return clock.next_cycle_evaluation_time ==
                clock.evaluation_time + smallest_step
        }
    }
    assert eval next_step(value: [1, _, 2]) == [true, _, true]
    ~~~

Rules:
    CAP-3, CAP-8, CRUN-3, TIME-8

documentation.text:
Fill the places in a constant format string.

`{}` consumes the next positional argument and `{name}` uses the given
name. Double a brace to write it literally. A place may add a specifier
after a colon, as in `{price:.2f}`.

| Value | Place |
| --- | --- |
| Integer, float, string or boolean | The type's numeric or text specifiers |
| Date, time, datetime or duration | The type's date or time directives and optional padding |
| Any other type | A place with no specifier, using its `convert<str>` |

Type Args:
    As: The types of the positional values, in supplied order.
    Ks: The types of the named values, keyed by their supplied names.

Args:
    fmt_str: The constant pattern containing literal text and places.
    args: The arguments that fill positional places.
    kwargs: The arguments that fill named places.

Options:
    - `not_valid: str`: text for an absent `Marked` payload. The default is
      `"<not valid>"`. Set it with `format{not_valid: "missing"}(...)`.
    - `ticked: str`: prefix for a marked place whose `Marked` argument ticked.
      The default is `"*"`. Set it with `format{ticked: "!"}(...)`.

Returns:
    The literal text with each place filled by its formatted value.

Raises:
    - `argument.constant`: the format string is not constant at compilation.
    - `format.syntax`: an unmatched brace.
    - `format.argument`: a place has no matching argument.
    - `format.unused`: an argument fills no place.
    - `format.specifier`: a place's type does not admit its specifier.
    - `operator.no_candidate`: a value has no required `convert<str>`.

Examples:
    ~~~hgl
    assert format("fill {} at {price:.2f}", 10, price: 101.5) == "fill 10 at 101.50"
    assert format("{{ready}}") == "{ready}"
    ~~~

Notes:
    See the [formatting reference](https://github.com/hhenson/hgl_core/blob/main/spec/formatting.md#reference)
    for the admitted specifiers and each type's default text.

Rules:
    FMT-1, FMT-2, FMT-3, FMT-4, FMT-5, FMT-7, FMT-9

documentation.text:
Format values where the call is evaluated in value code.

A `Marked` argument uses the specifiers of its payload type. If the
payload is absent, the place uses `not_valid` without applying the
specifier. In a place with `*`, a ticked argument also adds the
`ticked` prefix. A mark on any other argument rejects with
`format.specifier`. `{wall_time}` uses the process clock as a
`datetime`; `{engine_time}` rejects with `format.argument` in value code.

Type Args:
    As: The types of the positional values, in supplied order.
    Ks: The types of the named values, keyed by their supplied names.

Args:
    fmt_str: The constant format string.
    args: The arguments that fill positional places.
    kwargs: The arguments that fill named places.

Returns:
    The formatted text, including requested prefixes.

Examples:
    ~~~hgl
    let price = Marked<f64>(value: 101.5, ticked: true)
    assert format("mid {*:.1f}", price) == "mid *101.5"
    let absent = Marked<f64>(value: null, ticked: false)
    assert format{not_valid: "missing"}("mid {:.1f}", absent) == "mid missing"
    ~~~

Notes:
    See the [formatting reference](https://github.com/hhenson/hgl_core/blob/main/spec/formatting.md#reference)
    for the mark and clock place spellings.

Rules:
    FMT-4, FMT-7, FMT-9

documentation.text:
Write text to a process stream exactly as given.

The call adds no line ending and gives no result. It writes where it
is executed, in a value function or in a node handler. Its stream
text does not enter the run's record.

Args:
    text: The text to write, including any desired line ending.
    stream: The process stream. The default is `.out`.
    flush: Flush the stream before returning. The default is `false`,
        so the stream decides when the text is visible.

Examples:
    ~~~hgl
    write("ready\n", flush: true)
    write("warning\n", .err)
    ~~~

Notes:
    Use `format` to prepare text with values. See the
    [formatting reference](https://github.com/hhenson/hgl_core/blob/main/spec/formatting.md#reference).

Rules:
    OUT-1, OUT-2
